headline: Student protests close hundreds of French schools

sources.title: Hundreds of French schools remain closed as riot police clash with student protesters (France 24)
Public workers in France strike over pay as student protests turn violent (Al Jazeera)
School protests spread as fires, blockades deepen unrest in France (Al Jazeera)

chunks.text: High school students in France are protesting about [[overcrowded]] classrooms and [[teacher shortages]]. The protests {{broke out}} at schools in the Paris region during the week of September 21, 2026. This week they {{spilled over}} into other parts of the country, including Marseille, Strasbourg and Rennes. On Friday, October 2, about 400 of France's 3,700 high schools were {{shut down}}.

verbs.why: Laughter broke out in the room after the joke, and a fight broke out in the parking lot after the game. The protests broke out at high schools in the Paris region during the week of September 21.

Trouble at the stadium spilled over into nearby streets, and a fire in one field can spill over into the next. This week the protests spilled over into other parts of France, including Marseille, Strasbourg and Rennes.

verbs.correct: To close for a period of time
verbs.wrong: To be damaged during a protest

chunks.text: Students say 35 of them {{squeeze into}} a single classroom, without enough chairs for everyone. They are {{calling for}} more [[substitute teachers]], better buildings and more money for schools. Some also object to their [[class schedules]], to rooms that get too hot, and to a short [[lunch break]]. The government's draft 2027 budget raises [[education spending]] by 1.7 percent, to 65.53 billion euros. That increase does not {{keep up with}} [[inflation]].

verbs.correct: To rise as fast as something else
verbs.wrong: To be shared between many schools
verbs.why: Wages often fail to keep up with rent, and a small savings account rarely keeps up with rising prices. The 1.7 percent rise in education spending does not keep up with inflation.

chunks.text: In some places the protests have [[turned violent]]. Police used [[tear gas]] in Strasbourg, and trash cans were set on fire in Rennes. On October 1, the interior minister said police had [[detained]] more than 400 people, many of them [[minors]]. He said nothing [[excuses]] violence. The education minister said about 170 students and at least 65 school staff have been hurt. Officials are {{looking into}} [[claims]] of police violence. The education minister planned to {{sit down with}} unions, parents and student groups on Friday.

verbs.correct: To check the facts of something carefully
verbs.wrong: To make something known to the public
verbs.why: The airline is looking into why the flight was late, and the school is looking into a complaint from a parent. Officials are looking into claims of police violence against students.

verbs.correct: To meet someone to talk about a problem
verbs.wrong: To refuse a plan from the government
verbs.why: The coach sat down with each player after the season, and our landlord sat down with us to discuss the rent. The education minister planned to sit down with unions, parents and student groups on Friday.

chunks.text: The school protests come during a wider fight over [[public sector]] pay. On September 29, teachers, health workers and firefighters {{walked out}} across France. Unions said 300,000 people {{turned out}}, while police counted about 30,000 in Paris. Workers want a 6 percent [[raise]]. The government plans to {{hold down}} [[base pay]] in 2027 to save 2 billion euros. It would be the fourth [[pay freeze]] [[in a row]]. Teachers' unions are now {{stepping up}} the pressure with another strike on Tuesday, October 6.

verbs.why: Nurses walked out over long shifts, and factory workers walked out after their pay was cut. On September 29, teachers, health workers and firefighters walked out across France.

mainIdea.s: High school students angry about crowded classrooms and missing teachers have protested across France, closing about 400 schools. Public workers also held a strike against frozen pay.
mainIdea.why: Student protests over class sizes and teacher shortages spread from Paris and shut down about 400 schools, while public workers walked out over a pay freeze.

mainIdea.s: Students in France are protesting mainly against a plan to hold down public sector pay in 2027. Their marches started near Paris and have now spread to cities all over the country.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the students are calling for smaller classes, more teachers and better buildings. The pay freeze is the public workers' complaint.

mainIdea.s: The French education minister has announced a plan to make the school year two weeks shorter. Teachers' groups say the change will give students more time to rest in the summer.
mainIdea.why: There is no plan to shorten the school year. Students are protesting over crowded classrooms and teacher shortages, and about 400 high schools were shut down.

lines.text: Did you hear that about 400 high schools in France were {{shut down}} on Friday?
Student protests. They {{broke out}} near Paris a couple of weeks ago, and now they've {{spilled over}} into cities all over the country.
What are the students so angry about?
Crowded classrooms, mostly. They say 35 kids {{squeeze into}} one room, sometimes without enough chairs.
Thirty-five kids in one room? They must be [[packed like sardines]].
They're {{calling for}} more substitute teachers and better buildings. And the new budget only raises education spending by 1.7 percent.
So it doesn't even {{keep up with}} inflation. For a lot of students, that's probably [[the last straw]].
Right. And in some places it's turned violent. There was tear gas in Strasbourg, and hundreds of people were detained.
Sounds like things are [[at a boiling point]]. Is anyone {{looking into}} what the police did?
Officials are, yes. And the education minister planned to {{sit down with}} unions, parents and students on Friday.
Weren't there strikes this week, too?
On Tuesday, teachers, health workers and firefighters {{walked out}}. Unions said 300,000 people {{turned out}}. Police counted about 30,000 in Paris.
Well, [[depends who's counting]]. What do the workers want?
A 6 percent raise. The government wants to {{hold down}} their pay for the fourth year in a row.
And now the unions are {{stepping up}} the pressure?
Yes, teachers have another strike planned for next Tuesday. So [[all eyes on]] Tuesday.
